items.title: Measuring Students’ Attention Boundaries in GAI-Assisted Learning: Development and Validation of the GAI-Mediated Learning Boundary Scale and Latent Profile Analysis
items.abstract: The Generative AI (GAI) is reshaping the temporal and spatial organization of college learning and the perceived boundary crossing between teacher-assigned tasks and self-directed learning. This study developed and validated a scale to assess college students’ attention boundary management in GAI-mediated learning. Analyzing data from 1904 students at 3 colleges in China, the study established a five-dimensional structure: Flexibility, Fragmentation, Immersion, Positive Spillover, and Negative Spillover. Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis confirmed the scale’s psychometric properties. A Latent Profile Analysis identified four distinct student profiles, Protective, Strained, Overextended, and Engaged Permeability Management. Supplementary heterogeneity analyses examined differences across the four profiles by gender, grade level, university, purposes and duration of AI use, and other learning-related characteristics. Based on these, this study proposed profile-specific recommendations. The study provides a validated instrument for assessing students’ attention boundaries in GAI-mediated learning, identifies heterogeneous student profiles, and offers differentiated practical implications.

items.title: Occupational Health and Safety Risk Analysis of Six Engineering Laboratories Using an Activity-Based HIRARC Approach
items.abstract: Engineering laboratories combine high-energy machinery, live circuits, pressurised fluids and open flames with novice student operators, yet occupational health and safety in Indonesian higher education is still managed largely through academic rather than risk-based instruments. This study applies Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment and Risk Control (HIRARC) to six practicum laboratories of the Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, Universitas Tidar, using the practicum activity rather than the room as the unit of analysis. Hazards were identified through direct observation and document review and scored by an assessor panel on a 5 x 5 matrix with predefined severity and likelihood criteria. Three main findings emerge. First, the 27 activity-level hazards are dominated by mechanical sources, and nearly half of the activities (44%) are high risk before control. Second, risk profiles differ between laboratories: the machining-intensive Production Process, Welding and CNC laboratories carry the highest mean risk, while the single most severe activity is CNC operation with a running spindle, so mean-based and peak-based rankings point to different priorities. Third, combined engineering and administrative controls, each mapped to the Indonesian regulation that requires it, are expected by the assessor panel to bring every activity to the low band, an estimated mean reduction of 58.5%; this is a prospective panel estimate, not a result measured after implementation. The study contributes an activity-based, regulation-linked risk register that allows laboratories with different energy profiles to be compared on one scale and to be prioritised for safety investment.

items.title: On AI-augmented transformatizing in practice: protocols, quality criteria, and reporting standards for Human-AI Augmented Mixed Methods Research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping qualitative research, quantitative research, and mixed methods research, but practical guidance for conducting, evaluating, and reporting human–AI analytic collaboration remains underdeveloped. Building on AI-augmented transformatizing, a representational–recursive framework that conceptualizes AI as a participant in analytic re-representation rather than merely as a technical tool, this article advances a practice-oriented framework for Human-AI Augmented Mixed Methods Research. The article offers three integrated contributions. First, it proposes the AI-Augmented Transformatizing Protocol , a recursive workflow for preparing representations, for assigning human and AI analytic roles, for generating AI-assisted transformations, for conducting human critique, for refining findings, and for constructing meta-inferences. Second, it introduces quality criteria for assessing methodological rigor in human-AI augmented analysis, including representational fidelity, prompt traceability, recursive transparency, human oversight integrity, algorithmic reflexivity, convergence-divergence interrogation, meta-inferential robustness, and ethical accountability. Third, it presents reporting standards designed to help authors disclose AI systems, model versions, prompting procedures, analytic iterations, researcher interventions, validation/legitimation strategies, ethical safeguards, and limitations. These proposed methodological components are conceptual and practice-oriented rather than empirically validated; accordingly, the worked example illustrates their operational logic, whereas future research is needed to establish their empirical performance, including the validity and reliability of the HAAM-QAM. Rather than treating AI use as an optional efficiency enhancement, the framework positions human-AI collaboration as a structured methodological practice requiring explicit design, documentation, reflexivity, and accountability. By translating the theory of AI-augmented transformatizing into protocols, quality criteria, and reporting standards, this article provides methodologists, researchers, authors, reviewers, editors, graduate educators, mentors, and the like with practical guidance for conducting transparent, rigorous, and ethically responsible AI-augmented mixed methods research in psychology and related fields. In so doing, it extends current reporting guidelines and quality frameworks by addressing the distinctive representational, recursive, and ethical demands introduced when AI participates directly in analysis.

items.title: Perceptions of ChatGPT- and veterinarian-generated responses to pet owners’ medical questions
items.abstract: Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly significant in veterinary medicine, particularly in answering pet owners’ medical questions. AI’s integration could reduce veterinary professionals’ workload while improving access to medical advice. However, the reliability and quality of AI-generated responses compared to veterinarians’ remain unexplored. The objective was to determine whether AI-generated responses were perceived as comparable to veterinarian-generated responses. Methods This cross-sectional study analysed the answers to a sample of pet owners’ medical questions. Both a veterinarian and ChatGPT (GPT-4o, May 2024) provided answers, which were anonymised and presented in a survey distributed through mailing lists and public Facebook groups. Participants were asked to assess each response based on structure, quality, and empathy, using a five-point Likert scale. They then had to indicate whether they trusted the response, and which response they preferred. Results Over two-thirds of the 201 participants (68%) preferred the ChatGPT-generated answers ( p < 0.05), which were rated higher in structure, quality, and empathy. items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is fundamentally transforming academic work in higher education, reshaping teaching, research, data analysis, scholarly writing, and the resolution of increasingly complex academic tasks. Nevertheless, access to and use of AI does not automatically translate into effective AI-enabled academic capability. The gap between merely “using AI” and developing meaningful human–AI collaboration has therefore emerged as a critical issue in contemporary faculty development. This study aims to identify and empirically examine the factors shaping lecturers’ competence in effectively leveraging AI to address complex academic tasks in non-public universities in Vietnam. Particular attention is given to the roles of AI literacy, AI self-efficacy, Human–AI Collaboration Competence, and critical AI use, while examining institutional AI support as a potential moderating mechanism. A sequential mixed-methods design is proposed. The qualitative phase employs expert interviews and/or a Delphi process to develop, refine, and validate the conceptual dimensions and measurement indicators. The quantitative phase involves a large-scale survey of lecturers working in Vietnamese non-public universities. Structural equation modelling, using PLS-SEM or CB-SEM depending on data characteristics and model specifications, is employed to examine direct, mediating, and moderating relationships among the proposed constructs. The study is designed to identify the mechanisms through which AI literacy and AI self-efficacy are transformed into Human–AI Collaboration Competence, Critical AI Use, and AI-Enabled Academic Task Competence, ultimately contributing to lecturers’ capacity to perform complex academic tasks effectively. The proposed model provides an integrated explanation of how individual capabilities and institutional conditions jointly shape AI-enabled academic performance. The study proposes an AI-Enabled Academic Capability Development Model as a conceptual and empirical foundation for faculty development in the global digital era. The findings are expected to provide practical implications for non-public universities in designing AI competency development programmes, strengthening institutional AI support ecosystems, and promoting critical, responsible, and academically productive human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Physiological activation regimes reveal distinct autonomic mechanisms underlying operational performance under cognitive workload and stress
items.abstract: Human performance in safety-critical environments depends on the interaction between mental workload, stress, autonomic regulation, and behavior. This study investigated whether associations between heart rate variability (HRV) and performance varied across physiological activation ranges and operational contexts during a multi-task flight simulation implemented through the AeroStim platform. Forty-two healthy participants (25 ± 5 years) performed either a Workload-Only condition (WO; n = 20), comprising Tracking and System Monitoring tasks, or a Stress-Oriented condition (SO; n = 22), in which additional stress-inducing tasks were concurrently administered. ECG was continuously recorded using an EqVital wearable T-shirt. Linear and non-linear HRV indices were extracted and normalized within participants using Min-Max scaling. Gaussian Mixture Modeling of normalized SDNN identified three relative, subject-specific activation ranges ( Easy, Medium , and Hard ), with classification showing high stability across alternative normalization procedures. HRV-performance associations were assessed using Spearman correlations with permutation-based inference and Benjamini–Hochberg correction, while performance differences were evaluated using non-parametric tests. HRV-performance correlations varied across activation ranges and contexts; none passed FDR correction, so these should be considered exploratory. In WO, associations involved LF in the Easy range, SDNN, SD2, and LF in the Medium range, and SDNN, LF/HF, and Sample Entropy in the Hard range. In SO, associations in the Medium range extended to vagal, global variability, and non-linear complexity indices, while Hard-range associations mainly involved vagal and LF-related measures. Omission rate was lower at Medium than Easy activation in WO, providing partial support for an intermediate activation advantage, whereas no consistent performance optimum emerged across contexts. Between-condition comparisons revealed a robust speed-accuracy trade-off, with WO producing faster but less accurate responses and SO producing slower but more accurate responses. Sensitivity analysis further indicated that differences in exercise windows affected HRV metrics in a metric-dependent manner, with greater deviations generally observed for frequency-domain measures. The findings suggest that HRV-performance relationships are context- and activation-dependent rather than captured by a single universal marker. The results support the potential of regime-based, multimodal HRV monitoring for adaptive human-machine systems, while highlighting the need for standardized recording durations, independent autonomic markers, and validation across individuals and real operational environments.

items.title: Psychological Outcomes and Correlates Associated with Over-Reliance on Artificial Intelligence Tools: An Integrative Review
items.abstract: Abstract The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) has raised concerns about over-reliance and its psychological implications. This integrative review synthesised psychological outcomes and correlates associated with AI over-reliance and examined its conceptualisation and measurement. The review included 28 studies identified through database and citation searching. AI over-reliance was associated with depression, anxiety, psychological distress, and cognitive disengagement, while findings concerning well-being and self-related functioning, including self-efficacy and autonomy, were mixed and context-dependent. Evidence concerning social or relational functioning was particularly limited, with only one included study directly examining this domain as an outcome. Most evidence was cross-sectional and therefore did not establish temporal direction or causality. Notably, the only longitudinal study found that depression and anxiety predicted subsequent AI dependence, whereas dependence did not predict later depression or anxiety, suggesting that psychological distress may precede dependence. No consensus definition or measure emerged; studies examined reliance, psychological dependence, problematic or compulsive use, and addiction-like engagement. AI over-reliance is therefore best understood as an overarching, multidimensional concept. These findings highlight the need for clearer conceptual boundaries, standardised measurement, and longitudinal and experimental research. PROSPERO CRD420251038303.

items.title: Public-Sector AI Adoption Toolkit
items.abstract: A practical, vendor-neutral toolkit for public institutions that want employees to use generative AI tools in everyday written work while protecting institutional information and keeping a person accountable for every official product. It is designed for document-intensive teams such as internal control, internal audit, oversight, legal support, procurement, and program administration. The toolkit has five parts that can be used separately or together: Risk Classification Worksheet: four classes of AI use, from low risk to prohibited, with a step-by-step classification guide and a use register. Human-Review Protocol: de-identification and redaction before AI use, structured instructions with the PACTO method, a technical review checklist, validation and signature, and specialized assistants for repetitive processes. Role-Based Curriculum Outline: a twelve-hour course in three sessions with step-by-step hands-on practice. Pilot Measurement Template: baselines defined in advance and reports that keep observations separate from causal conclusions. Facilitator Guide: preparing internal staff to deliver later cohorts. The toolkit systematizes practices the author developed in Brazilian public administration from 2024 to 2026, described in Gomes (2026), arXiv:2606.01517.

items.title: Regulating the Self, Orchestrating Interaction, and Acting Responsibly: A Positive Computing Perspective on Digital Wellbeing in GenAI-IDLE
items.abstract: This project examines digital wellbeing (DW) in generative artificial intelligence-mediated informal digital learning of English (GenAI-IDLE). Drawing on the positive computing framework, the study investigates the roles of GenAI-supported self-regulated learning, student–student interaction, student–teacher interaction, student–GenAI interaction, and perceived GenAI responsibility in shaping DW among Chinese EFL learners. Data were collected from 281 participants and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) to examine both predictive relationships and necessary conditions. The project materials include the English and Chinese versions of the measures used in the study and related analytical results. These materials are made openly available to support transparency, reproducibility, and future research on GenAI-mediated informal language learning and digital wellbeing.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning with Comparative Evidence for Social Intelligence
items.abstract: Developing socially intelligent AI remains heavily dependent on human-annotated data, limiting the scale and breadth of social understanding models can acquire. Methods that derive training signals from unlabeled data offer a path beyond this dependence, but social predictions lack the verification oracles available in mathematics and coding. Moreover, core social targets such as affect, intent, preference, and pragmatic meaning are often ambiguous. The same behavior can support multiple plausible interpretations, making it difficult to verify which is best supported. To address this challenge, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Comparative Evidence (RLCE), a reinforcement learning method that learns social understanding from unlabeled training data without constructing rewards from ground-truth annotations. Given distinct answers in a rollout group, RLCE constructs evidence tests that identify observable evidence favoring an answer over another, validates these tests against the input sample, and aggregates test outcomes to determine the best-supported interpretation. Tests are regenerated as the policy produces new answers, enabling them to evolve with the policy. Across four benchmarks spanning affect, pragmatics, communicative intent, and preference, RLCE attains the strongest performance among seven methods that use no ground-truth training labels for rewards, including consensus, policy LLM-judge verification, multimodal co-evolution, and rubric-based rewards. Gains over the strongest baseline reach up to +18.93 points. Analyses further show that RLCE exhibits a larger share of reward variation between correct and incorrect predictions than compared rubric methods, can overturn erroneous policy-derived preferences, and benefits from pairwise test construction, compositional test aggregation, and on-policy test evolution.

items.title: Relational Foundations of Sustainable Working Life: A Critical Integrative Review and Multilevel Framework of Trust, Social Competences, and Belonging
items.abstract: Socially sustainable working life requires more than continued employment or short-term performance; it depends on relational conditions that preserve health, voice, inclusion, and capability over time. This critical integrative review examines trust, social competences, belonging, and psychological safety across individual, interactional, team, organisational, and institutional levels. A 70-source seed corpus was audited, 38 non-redundant sources were retained, two nearest-model publications were added, and a documented public update screened 30 candidates identified through PubMed/PMC, EconBiz, publisher and DOI records, and citation chaining. Ten new articles were included, yielding 50 substantive sources. The review compares RFSWL with workplace social sustainability, swAge, capability-based sustainable employability, relational coordination, inclusion, psychological safety, and multilevel trust models. Its contribution is a new integrative configuration rather than new constructs: trust enables warranted vulnerability, social competences enable reciprocal coordination and repair, and belonging enables recognised membership without assimilation. It proposes to explain why favourable relational perceptions can coexist with silence or unequal participation when they fail to become reciprocally enacted and institutionally protected team processes. Through repeated interaction, these foundations may generate team trust climate, relational coordination, inclusive climate, and psychological safety, while governance, work design, employment security, digital control, and status relations condition their effects. Six propositions specify enabling, failure, distributional, and feedback pathways for multilevel longitudinal research.

items.title: Resilience Evaluation of Urban Tunnel Operations Based on Multi-Source Data and Explainable Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As critical nodes in urban transportation networks, the operational resilience of urban tunnels directly affects roadway network efficiency and public safety. Existing studies on tunnel resilience exhibit deficiencies in the attention paid to routine incidents, the interpretability of evaluation methods, and the robustness of underlying data. To address these gaps, this paper constructs a three-layer resilience evaluation framework (pre-event, during-event, and post-event) based on 1123 accident records, hourly traffic flow data, and expert scoring data from 10 urban tunnels in Shanghai in 2024. The framework integrates the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and min–max normalization to derive comprehensive resilience scores. Furthermore, two explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques—SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) feature importance analysis and K-means clustering—are introduced to identify key drivers of resilience differentiation and typical resilience patterns, respectively. Empirical results reveal that (1) half of the 10 tunnels achieve a B-level rating or above, while C/D-level tunnels still account for 50%, indicating considerable room for improvement; (2) SHAP analysis suggests that during-event absorption capacity contributes most significantly to resilience differences (50.24%), with the average traffic reduction rate being the most influential single indicator within this model; and (3) K-means clustering classifies the tunnels into four patterns: high-resilience balanced type, pre-event weak type, post-event weak type, and during-event weak type, each corresponding to distinct resilience enhancement strategies. The methodological framework developed in this paper effectively enables the quantification, interpretation, and pattern recognition of tunnel resilience, providing data-driven decision support for urban tunnel operation and management. It should be noted that the A–D ratings are sensitive to the normalization method: under an alternative normalization, 7 out of 10 tunnels change grade. The ratings should therefore be interpreted as relative to the selected sample rather than as absolute performance levels.

items.title: Responsible AI Governance and Talent Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping talent development through skills analytics, personalized learning, AI-supported coaching, competency assessment, career development, internal mobility, and workforce planning. These applications can expand access to development and strengthen workforce capability, but they also create legal, ethical, social, and environmental responsibilities that efficiency-oriented approaches do not fully address. This study examines how ten influential global AI governance instruments align with the five dimensions of Socially Responsible Artificial Intelligence (SRAI): economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic, and environmental responsibility. Using comparative policy analysis, the study evaluates policy ideas, institutional force, and implementation instruments and then translates the observed patterns into governance requirements for AI-enabled talent development. The analysis shows strong convergence around human oversight, transparency, fairness, accountability, and capability building, while employee participation, equitable access to development, community learning, and environmental accountability remain unevenly institutionalized. Building on these findings, the article develops an SRAI-informed governance architecture linking global norms to learning-data governance, fair competency assessment, explainable career recommendations, continuous reskilling, worker voice, community capability building, and resource-aware learning systems. The framework positions responsible talent development as an organizational mechanism for creating workforce capability, lifelong employability, social inclusion, and sustainable value, thereby connecting AI governance with Common-Good Human Resource Management.

items.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
items.abstract: Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making. Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making. Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings. This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

items.title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
items.abstract: Generative AI weakens the link between assessed performance and the cognitive processes that educational work is expected to reflect. This paper examines observable traces of those processes in a sample of 150 student-AI conversations. The analysis uses the concept of epistemic ownership as an interpretive framework, focusing on three dimensions that can become visible in interaction: Direction, Integration, and Evaluation. The results show that similar assessed performance can coexist with substantially different observable patterns of cognitive participation. Assignment scores therefore provide information about assessed outcomes but do not recover how cognitive work was distributed between student and AI during the interaction. The study provides an empirical basis for asking how assessment should incorporate evidence about cognitive process, rather than relying exclusively on the quality of the resulting product.

items.title: Seeing through the Eyes of AI: Situated Explainability in Augmented Reality
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI) enables humans to understand and interpret decisions of AI models. Instead of having a black box, explainability supports humans in understanding AI models' behavior. Existing explainable AI approaches often present explanations on 2D displays using pre-recorded data, requiring users to relate the displayed information back to the physical objects and real world locations involved in a model's decision. Users are forced to decouple data exploration and capture from AI model interpretation. For AI systems that work within physical environments, this separation can make explanations difficult to interpret in context. We propose using Augmented Reality (AR) to enhance the understanding of AI models by enabling spatial explainability information directly in a user's workspace, in real time, as they explore the world. We show how known explainability methods can be applied in AR and provide insights into user experiences with such an application.

items.title: SGA-based volleyball teaching with explicit life skills instruction is associated with technical-tactical, psychosocial, and motivational improvements in school students
items.abstract: This quasi-experimental study examined whether a school volleyball unit based on the Step-Game-Approach model combined with explicit life skills teaching (SGA + LS) was associated with changes in technical-tactical performance, life skills, motivation, and perception of success. Eighty-eight students aged 10–12 years participated in a quasi-experimental repeated-measures design with three groups: SGA + LS, direct instruction, and control. The intervention comprised 18 Physical Education classes. Outcomes were assessed before and/or after the intervention using IAD-VB, Life Skills Scale for Sport, Behavioral Regulation in Sport Questionnaire, and Perception of Success Questionnaire. Generalized Estimating Equations tested group, time, and group×time effects. Significant group × time interactions that remained significant after false discovery rate correction were observed for goal setting, Wald χ²(2) = 11.875, pFDR=0.009, time management, Wald χ²(2) = 10.203, pFDR=0.014, and communication, Wald χ²(2) = 7.538, pFDR=0.044. items.title: Smart Automation For Ergonomic Risk Management In Sustainable Garment Manufacturing: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Garment manufacturing is a labor-intensive industry characterized by routine activities and awkward postures with physical demands, which makes employees vulnerable to a series of ergonomic risks. These risks negatively impact worker health and productivity. Emerging technologies like smart automation and robotics provide relevant solutions to mitigate this, improving workplace safety and overall working conditions. However, there are limitations and gaps in existing literature on ergonomics risk mitigation in garment manufacturing. These pertain to common ergonomics risks, their factors and impact, ergonomics risk mitigation strategies, and technological solutions. To identify these gaps, this study conducted a systematic literature review of 102 peer-reviewed articles published from 2010 to 2025 by synthesizing ergonomic risk and its factors, their effects on workers, and technological and strategic mitigation approaches. To ensure a focused review, four inclusion criteria were applied: (1) papers published between 2010 and 2025, (2) alignment with disciplines like Engineering, (3) inclusion of only research articles, (4) English-language articles. The review revealed that common ergonomic risks in garment manufacturing such as repetitive motion, awkward postures, and prolonged static positions, are major contributors to musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). Furthermore, the ergonomic risk factors were physical, environmental, and organizational. Moreover, these risks have a significant effect on workers' health and overall operational efficiency. Consequently, smart automation technologies like robotic systems, wearable exoskeletons, and ergonomically designed workstations emerge as relevant interventions for those risks. This study’s findings provide evidence-based insights to improve workers' health and productivity, and future directions and implications for managers, policymakers, and practitioners in garment manufacturing. Keywords: Ergonomics, Garment Manufacturing Industry, Innovation, Risk Management, Smart Automation, and Sustainable development

items.title: Students’ conceptions of artificial intelligence and machine learning in K–12 education: a systematic review
items.abstract: Background and context Knowing students’ conceptions of computer science phenomena is essential for the design of teaching–learning settings and instruments. They are particularly interesting in teaching artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) concepts. Therefore, a comprehensive synthesis focused on K–12 is essential to provide educators with actionable conceptions for curriculum design and assessment.Objective We investigate common conceptions of AI/ML in K–12 and to which curricular concepts these can be assigned. We also examine how conceptions vary across age/grade groups and the data collection/evaluation methods employed. This study uniquely synthesizes fragmented research on students’ conceptions of AI/ML into a unified snapshot, offering a systematic mapping that informs curriculum recommendations.Method A systematic literature review according to PRISMA is used to identify the relevant studies. We analyzed the selected literature, extracted the student conceptions, and classified them according to the curricular concepts.Findings We identified 27 relevant studies (from 2007 to 2024) including the conceptions of 1,077 K–12 students from 30 different countries. In addition, our data includes further information on the type of school, age/grade levels, genders and nationalities, the availability of the collected data, and the survey and evaluation methods used. We took a closer look at 29 of the 409 resulting, highly prevalent conceptions, which stand out due to their frequent occurrence.Implications Our findings may be useful for determining in which grade levels interventions targeting specific concepts would be most effective. This could also be used to study the development of these conceptions or developing assessments.
